question: What are the common fungal diseases affecting Uttar Pradesh Pea and how can they be managed?
final_answer:
Fungal diseases are among the most common and damaging problems in pea cultivation, particularly in Uttar Pradesh where humid conditions favour disease development. Major fungal diseases include powdery mildew, rust, downy mildew, and leaf blight, which can significantly reduce pod formation and seed yield if not managed properly.

1. Powdery Mildew
Symptoms:
- White to greyish powdery growth appears on leaves, stems, pods, and other plant parts.
- Infected plants show stunted growth, reduced flowering, poor pod setting, and lower yields.
- Severe infection reduces grain quality and market value.

Management:
Cultural control: 
- Use healthy, certified seeds from disease-free areas.
- Follow crop rotation with non-host crops such as cereals or vegetables.
- Maintain proper field sanitation by removing infected plant debris after harvest.
- Avoid excessive nitrogen application, as it promotes succulent growth that favours disease development.
- Ensure balanced fertilizer application for better plant health and resistance.

Chemical Control:
Spray any one of the following fungicides at 20-day intervals until disease incidence is controlled:

Propiconazole 25% EC @ 200 ml/acre (PHI - 36 days)
Hexaconazole 5% EC @ 400 ml/acre (PHI - 37 days)
Carbendazim 50% WP @ 200 g/acre (PHI - 21 days)

2. Rust
Symptoms:
- Small yellowish-brown pustules appear on leaves, stems, and pods.
- Pustules later turn reddish-brown and develop into black spots.
- Affected plants become weak, produce fewer flowers, and yield less grains.

Management:
Cultural control:
- Collect and destroy infected plant debris after harvest.
- Remove volunteer pea plants and weeds that harbour pathogens.
- Practice deep summer ploughing to expose overwintering stages of rust fungi.
- Grow resistant varieties wherever available.
- Apply balanced fertilizers and avoid excess nitrogen, which encourages disease development.

Chemical Control:
Spray any one of the recommended fungicides at 15-day intervals:

Propiconazole 25% EC @ 100–125 ml/acre (PHI - 36 days) 
Zineb 75% WP @ 600–800 g/acre (PHI - 30 days)
Mancozeb 75% WP @ 600 g/acre (PHI - 35 days)

3. Downy Mildew
Symptoms:
- Yellow spots appear on upper leaf surfaces while white fungal growth develops on lower leaf surfaces.
- Leaves gradually dry up and fall prematurely.
- Plants remain stunted, flower poorly, and produce small, shriveled pods containing underdeveloped seeds.

Management:
Cultural control:
- Use certified, disease-free seed.
- Follow crop rotation with non-leguminous crops.
- Remove and destroy infected plant residues after harvest.
- Avoid overhead irrigation; maintain good drainage to prevent water stagnation.
- Monitor fields regularly during cool, moist weather when disease pressure is high.

Chemical Control:
Spray any one of the fungicides at 15-day intervals:

Propicon唑 25% EC @ 100–200 ml/acre (PHI - 49 days)
Hexaconazole 5% EC @ 200 ml/acre
Trifloxystrobin + Tebuconazole 75 WG @ 120 g/acre

4. Leaf Blight
Symptoms:
- Brown to dark brown lesions appear on leaves, stems, and pods.
- Lesions enlarge rapidly and may merge together, causing extensive defoliation.
- Severely affected plants lose vigour, produce few pods, and yield substantially reduced grain quantities.

Management:
Cultural control:
- Use certified, healthy seed.
- Follow crop rotation with non-leguminous cereal crops.
- Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest.
- Avoid excessive nitrogen application because lush foliage increases disease severity.
- Maintain proper field sanitation and remove alternate host plants around the field.

Chemical Control:
Spray any one of the foliar fungicides at 15-day intervals:

Propiconazole 25% EC @ 200 ml per acre (PHI - 36 days)
Hexaconazol 5% EC @ 400 ml per acre (PHI - 37 days)
Carbapenem 75% WP @ 200 g per acre (PHI - 21 days)

Safety Precautions
Always wear protective clothing including gloves, mask, goggles, and boots while handling fungicides.
Avoid spraying during windy conditions or peak sunshine hours.
Do not eat, drink, or smoke while mixing or applying chemicals.
Wash hands thoroughly with soap after handling pesticides.
Store pesticides safely away from children, livestock, food items, and drinking water sources.
Dispose of empty containers responsibly according to local regulations.

Conclusion
Effective management of fungal diseases in pea requires an integrated approach combining cultural practices, timely monitoring, and need-based chemical intervention. Regular field inspection, removal of infected plant material, balanced nutrition, and adherence to recommended fungicide schedules help minimize disease spread and protect pea productivity.

question: What is the recommended nutrient management practice for bean cultivation?
final_answer:

Proper nutrient management helps improve root development, nodulation, flowering, pod formation, and overall productivity in beans.

question: What fungicide should I spray to control diseases in paddy crop?
final_answer:
Fungicides are essential for controlling fungal diseases in paddy crops, which can significantly impact yield and grain quality. Understanding the correct fungicide to use is crucial for effective disease management.
 
Common Fungal Diseases in Paddy:
The major fungal diseases affecting paddy include Blast (caused by Pyricularia oryzae), Sheath Blight (Rhizoctonia solani), Brown Spot (Helminthosporium oryzae), and Sheath Rot (Sarocladium oryzae). Each disease manifests distinct symptoms and requires specific management approaches.
 
Blast Disease: Appears as diamond-shaped lesions on leaves with gray centers and brown margins. Neck blast affects the panicle neck, causing it to break and resulting in chaffy grains.
 
Sheath Blight: Characterized by oval or elliptical greenish-gray lesions on leaf sheaths near the water line, which later enlarge and turn brown with a purple border.
 
Brown Spot: Shows small, circular-to-oval spots on leaves that are uniformly brown or have a light center with reddish-brown margins.
 
Integrated Disease Management:
Cultural Practices:
 1. Use certified disease-free seeds from reliable sources
 2. Treat seeds with Carbendazim 50% WP @ 2 g/kg seed before sowing
 3. Maintain proper spacing (20x15 cm for transplanted paddy) to ensure good air circulation
 4. Avoid excessive nitrogen application, which promotes fungal growth
 5. Drain fields periodically to reduce humidity levels
 6. Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
 7. Practice crop rotation with non-host crops
 8. Balance nitrogen application; avoid excess nitrogen, which increases disease susceptibility
 
Chemical Control Measures:
For Blast Disease:
Spray Propiconazole 25 EC at 200 ml per acre mixed in 200 liters of water. This should be applied when the disease appears and repeated if necessary.
 
For Sheath Blight:
Apply Tebuconazole 25 WG at 200 grams per acre mixed in 200 liters of water during early morning or evening hours. Ensure thorough coverage of the leaf sheaths where the fungus typically develops.
 
For Brown Spot:
Use Hexaconazole 5 EC at 200 ml per acre mixed with 200 liters of water. Apply this spray during the initial appearance of the disease.
 
Safety Precautions:
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Always wear gloves, masks, goggles, and protective clothing while handling and spraying chemicals.
Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): Observe the PHI strictly. For most fungicides used in paddy, this is typically 15-21 days depending on the chemical used.
 
Application Guidelines:
Ensure uniform coverage of both upper and lower surfaces of the leaves. Spray during calm weather conditions (morning or late afternoon) to prevent drift and runoff losses.
 
Monitoring and Follow-Up:
Regularly monitor your field for new infections. If disease pressure continues despite treatment, consider adjusting cultural practices such as changing fertilizer schedules or altering planting dates.

question: What are the best practices and methods for effective weed management in onion cultivation?
final_answer:
Weeds compete with onion plants for nutrients, moisture, sunlight, and space, particularly during the early stages of crop growth. Since onions have a shallow root system and slow initial growth, they cannot compete effectively with weeds. Therefore, timely and integrated weed management is essential to ensure healthy crop establishment, proper bulb development, and higher bulb yield.

1. Cultural and Mechanical Weed Management

You should maintain a weed-free field throughout the crop growth period, especially during the first 45–60 days after transplanting, which is the critical period of crop-weed competition in onion. Carry out 3–4 hand weeding or hoeings as required to remove weeds before they compete with the crop. Regular field monitoring and timely removal of newly emerging weeds help improve nutrient availability, conserve soil moisture, and promote healthy bulb development.

2. Chemical Weed Management

For effective early-season weed control, apply a pre-emergence herbicide within 3 days after transplanting on moist soil. You may use Pendimethalin 30% EC @ 2.5–3.5 litres/ha (1.0–1.4 litres/acre) or Oxyfluorfen 23.5% EC @ 600–1000 mL/ha (240–400 mL/acre). Mix the recommended herbicide in approximately 750 litres of water per hectare (300 litres/acre) and spray uniformly over the field. After herbicide application, avoid disturbing the soil because breaking the herbicide layer reduces its effectiveness. If weeds emerge later in the season, follow up with hand weeding to keep the field weed-free throughout the crop growth period.

3. Integrated Weed Management

The most effective approach is to combine timely hand weeding with the recommended pre-emergence herbicides. Regular crop monitoring and immediate removal of newly emerged weeds help minimize competition between the crop and weeds. This integrated approach provides better weed suppression than either method alone while conserving soil moisture and improving bulb yield.

Conclusion

Effective weed management in onion cultivation requires an integrated approach that combines timely cultural practices, mechanical weeding, and recommended herbicides. Maintaining a weed-free field during the critical early growth stage helps reduce competition for nutrients, moisture, and sunlight, promotes healthy bulb development, and improves overall productivity. Following these recommended practices ensures better crop health, efficient resource utilization, and higher onion yields.

Safety Precautions
Wear gloves, mask, protective clothing, and eye protection while handling and spraying herbicides.
Spray only at the recommended dose and dilution; do not exceed the prescribed concentration.
Avoid spraying during strong winds or rainfall to prevent drift and runoff losses.
Do not eat, drink, or smoke while preparing or applying herbicides.
Keep children, livestock, and unauthorized persons away from treated fields until the spray has dried.
Dispose of empty containers safely according to local regulations and never reuse them for household purposes.

question: What is the correct method and dosage for applying Blitox and Boron to coconut palms to ensure effective nutrient management and disease control in West Bengal?
final_answer:
Boron deficiency and fungal diseases such as fruit rot and bud rot are common problems in coconut palms in West Bengal, particularly during the monsoon season. Timely nutrient application and preventive fungicide sprays help maintain healthy palms and reduce yield losses.

Boron Application:
- Apply Borax @ 50 grams per palm per year.
- Broadcast the borax uniformly in a circular basin around the palm, about 1.8 meters away from the trunk (within the fertilizer application zone).
- Apply once annually, preferably at the onset of the monsoon along with the recommended fertilizer application.

Disease Management Using Copper Oxychloride 50% WP:

Fruit Rot and Fruit Drop:
Fungal attacks cause fruits to drop prematurely. Affected young fruits develop blackish-brown spots near the cap/surface.

Management:
- Dissolve Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 4 g per litre of water.
- Spray the developing bunches and fruits thoroughly.
- Repeat the spray at 15-day intervals if disease persists.

Bud Rot Disease:
This is also known as crown rot. The young leaves of the tree get infected, bend at the base, and eventually break off. If the attack is severe, the tree dies. The intensity of this disease increases during the monsoon season.

Management: 
Spray the tree thoroughly 3 to 4 times at 15-day intervals before or during the monsoon using a mixture of 4 grams of Copper Oxychloride 50% WP per liter of water, along with 1 gram of Carbendazim 50% WP per liter of water.

Precautions:
- Apply borax only at the recommended dose, as excess boron may cause toxicity.
- Ensure thorough coverage of the crown, spindle, and fruit bunches while spraying fungicides.
- Spray during calm weather, preferably in the early morning or late afternoon.
- Avoid spraying before rainfall to prevent wash-off.
- Wear gloves, a face mask, protective clothing, and goggles while handling fungicides.
- Prepare fresh spray solution and use it on the same day.

The application of Borax @ 50 g per palm annually helps correct boron deficiency and promotes healthy growth and nut development. For effective management of fruit rot, fruit drop, and bud rot, spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 4 g per litre of water, and for bud rot, use Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 4 g per litre of water along with 1 gram of Carbendazim 50% WP per liter of water at 15-day intervals. Timely nutrient management, preventive fungicide application, and good field sanitation are essential for maintaining healthy coconut palms and improving productivity.

question: How can we manage kala Tella (black aphid infestation) in mustard?

question: What is the best way to control leaf curl virus in Bengal gram (chickpea) crops?
final_answer:
In Haryana, leaf curl virus is a major problem in crops like cotton, but it is not a significant issue in Bengal gram. 

Leaf curling symptoms in Bengal gram are usually caused by sucking pest infestation (such as aphids, jassids, and thrips) or due to diseases like Chickpea stunt disease (dwarfism) and wilt, rather than a true leaf curl virus. Therefore, management should focus on controlling sucking pests and maintaining proper crop health.

Sucking Pest cause leaf curl in Bengal gram (chickpea):

Identification & Symptoms
-Aphids : Colonies on tender shoots and leaves, Leaf curling, yellowing, and sticky honeydew and Sooty mold development.
-Jassids : Yellowing at leaf margins (“hopper burn”),Downward leaf curling and leaves become brittle and stunted.
-Thrips : Silvery streaks on leaves, Upward/longitudinal curling and distortion and Flower drop and poor pod set.

Monitoring :
-Regular field scouting, Count pests on leaves and observe symptoms.
-Use yellow sticky traps (aphids, jassids) and blue sticky traps (thrips)

Cultural Practices:
-Synchronous sowing: Grow crop at the same time in the area to reduce pest buildup
-Deep summer ploughing: Expose and destroy soil-borne pest stages
-Optimum spacing & thinning: Avoid dense crop to reduce pest-friendly microclimate
-Balanced fertilization: Apply fertilizers based on soil test; avoid excess nitrogen
-Intercropping: Use crops like coriander/mustard to conserve natural enemies
-Border/trap crops: Plant garlic or marigold to reduce pest incidence
-Insectary plants: Maintain flowering plants (fennel, carrot, etc.) to support beneficial insects
 
 Biological Control :
 -Conserve natural enemies: Green lacewing (Chrysoperla carnea),
Ladybird beetles and Hover flies.
- These predators naturally reduce sucking pest populations.
 
Biopesticide control : Spray NSKE 5% or Azadirachtin 0.03% (Neem oil based) at the pre-flowering stage.
 
 Diseases cause Leaf curling in Bengal gram (chickpea):
Wilt (Ukheda) Disease in Bengal gram
 Symptoms
-Appears 3–6 weeks after sowing
-Sudden wilting of plants, leaves droop and may curl but often remain green initially.
-Partial or complete plant drying
- On splitting the stem, vascular tissues show brown to black discoloration
Infected plants can be easily uprooted.

Management Practices
Cultural Practices
-Sow crop at recommended time (after mid-October in Haryana)
-Maintain optimum soil moisture.
-Follow crop rotation with non-host crops.
-Ensure proper drainage 

Resistant Varieties : Haryana Gram 1, Haryana Gram 3, Haryana Gram 5, Haryana Kabuli 1, Haryana Kabuli 2.

Seed Treatment: Treat seeds with Carbendazim @ 2–2.5 g/kg seed (fungicide) or Trichoderma viride @ 4 g/kg seed (biological control)

 Integrated Approach:
 - Combine the above cultural, varietal, biological, and chemical measures for an effective and sustainable management of leaf curl  in Bengal gram.
 - Monitor the crop regularly and be vigilant for any recurring disease outbreaks.

question: What is the maximum subsidy available for agricultural machinery under the SMAM scheme in Kerala?

question: Could you please provide guidance on preventing the root worm pest in Bengal gram cultivation?
final_answer:
Root worm is not a major pest of Bengal gram (chickpea). The most important insect pests affecting chickpea are the pod borer and hairy caterpillar. These pests damage leaves, flowers, pods, and developing seeds, resulting in reduced yield and quality.

1. Pod Borer
Symptoms:
-Young larvae initially feed on tender shoots and young leaves.
-Later they bore into flower buds and fruits, causing severe damage to developing pods.
-Severe infestation results in heavy yield loss.
-The adult moth is brownish-yellow with black spots on its forewings.

Management:
Cultural Control:
-Sow the crop at the recommended time.
-Avoid excessive nitrogen application, as it encourages lush growth that attracts pests.
-Maintain proper field sanitation by removing weeds and alternate host plants.
-Install pheromone traps @ 4–5 traps/acre for monitoring adult moths.
-Use light traps @ 1 trap/acre during evening hours to attract and kill adult moths.
-Apply neem cake @ 80 kg/acre before sowing.
-Practice intercropping with cowpea or maize to reduce pest incidence.
-Encourage natural enemies such as parasitoids and predators through ecological engineering.

Biological Control:
-Conserve beneficial insects like ladybird beetles, lacewings, spiders, and predatory bugs.
-Release Trichogramma chilonis @ 2 lakh/acre.
-Treat seed with Beauveria bassiana @ 2 g/kg seed.
-Apply entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) @ 20 crore infective juveniles/acre.

Chemical Control:
Spray any one of the following insecticides when pest population reaches economic threshold level:
-Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC @ 60 ml/acre in 200 litres water
-Deltamethrin 2.8% EC @ 120 ml/acre in 200 litres water

2. Hairy Caterpillar
Symptoms:
-Hairy caterpillars feed voraciously on leaves, stems, and developing pods.
-They scrape leaf tissues, leaving only the veins, which causes defoliation.
-In severe cases, entire crops may be destroyed due to continuous feeding.
-The caterpillars have dense hairs covering their body, giving them a woolly appearance.

Management:
Cultural Control:
-Regularly monitor fields from flowering stage onwards.
-Collect and destroy egg masses and early-stage larvae manually.
-Remove heavily infested plant parts whenever possible.
-Keep bunds clean and free from weed hosts.
-Adopt timely sowing to avoid peak larval emergence.
-Plant border crops such as sorghum, maize, or pearl millet around the field to reduce pest movement.

Mechanical Control:
-Manually collect and destroy large caterpillars during early stages.
-Set up bonfires during evening hours to attract and kill adult moths.
-Uproot and burn infested plants containing larvae.
-Install bird perches @ 10/acre to encourage predatory birds.

Biological Control:
-Conserve natural enemies such as spiders, wasps, dragonflies, praying mantids, fire ants, and other beneficial organisms.
-Release Trichogramma spp. @ 2 lakh/acre.
-Apply Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki @ 600 g/acre.
-Apply entomopathogenic fungi such as Metarhizium anisopliae @ 2 kg/acre.

Chemical Control:
-Spray Quinalphos 25% EC @ 400 ml/acre in 200 litres water.
-Alternatively, spray Chlorpyrifos 20% EC @ 400 ml/acre in the same volume of water.

Safety Precautions:
-Wear gloves, mask, protective clothing, and eye protection while handling pesticides.
-Follow label instructions regarding dosage, waiting period, and safety measures.
-Do not eat, drink, or smoke during pesticide mixing and spraying operations.
-Store pesticides safely away from children, livestock, food materials, and drinking water sources.
-Wash hands, face, and exposed skin thoroughly after spraying.
-Dispose of empty containers safely according to local regulations.

Conclusion:
Pod borer and hairy caterpillar are serious insect pests of Bengal gram that can cause significant yield losses if left unmanaged. Regular field monitoring, conservation of natural enemies, use of biological control agents, adoption of cultural practices, and need-based application of recommended insecticides help effectively manage these pests and protect crop productivity.

For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

question: What are the recommended dosages and application methods for Fipronil 4% + Acetamiprid 4% SC in Chilli cultivation to manage common pests in Madhya Pradesh?
final_answer:
Fipronil 4% + Acetamiprid 4% SC is a combination insecticide used for the management of sucking pests and leaf-eating caterpillars in chilli. It provides effective control against important insect pests such as aphids, whiteflies, thrips, red spider mites, and fruit borers.

Recommended Dosage:
For the management of sucking pests and leaf-eating caterpillARS, apply Fipronil 4% + Acetamipride 4% SC @ 200 ml per hectare (81 ml/acre) mixed in 500 litres of water per hectare (202 litres/acre). The waiting period before harvest is 7 days.

Application Method:
Spray uniformly on both upper and lower surfaces of leaves using a knapsack sprayer or power sprayer fitted with a flat-fan nozzle. Ensure thorough coverage of foliage to achieve effective pest control.

Target Pests:

Aphids: Small green insects that suck sap from tender shoots and young leaves.
Whiteflies: Tiny yellowish-white insects found mainly on the underside of leaves.
Thrips: Minute black or brown insects that scrape plant tissues and cause silvery patches on leaves.
Red Spider Mite: Red-coloured mites that feed by sucking cell contents from leaves.
Fruit Borer: Caterpillar-like larvae bore into fruits and feed inside them, causing rotting and poor market quality.

Safety Precautions
Wear gloves, mask, protective clothing, and eye protection while handling pesticides.
Do not eat, drink, or smoke during pesticide application.
Avoid spraying during strong winds or rainfall.
Follow the recommended dose strictly; avoid overdosing.
Observe the prescribed pre-harvest interval (PHI) before harvesting the crop.

Conclusion

Fipronil 4% + Acetamidiprid 4% SC is an effective insecticide formulation for managing sucking pests and leaf-eating caterpillars in chillii. Apply it at 200 ml per hectare (81 mL/acre) mixed in 500 litres of spray solution per hectare (202 L/acre), ensuring uniform coverage of both upper and lower leaf surfaces. This formulation helps protect plants from damage caused by aphids, whiteflies, thrips, red spider-mites, and fruit borers, thereby improving yield and fruit quality.

question: How can weed management be effectively managed in groundnut?
final_answer:
Effective weed management is critical during the early stages of groundnut cultivation to ensure that nutrients, sunlight, and moisture are available solely to the crop. 

To ensure effective weed management, follow the Integrated Weed Management Strategies. Integrated Weed Management (IWM) in groundnut combines cultural, mechanical, and chemical methods to effectively control weeds while reducing dependence on any single approach. Because groundnut is a slow-growing crop in its early stages, it is highly susceptible to weed competition, making the first 45 days after sowing the critical period for management

These are some common weeds that can be seen in the Groundnut field:
-Indian mallow
-Pigweed
-Mexican poppy
-Nut sedge
-Crowfoot grass
-Crab grass
-Bran Yard gr-ass
-Love grass
-Spurge
-Jews mellow
-Button plant
-Common purslan
-Gaint pigweed

Integrated Weed Management (IWM) in Groundnut

1. Preventive Methods
-Prevent movement of weed seeds through irrigation water, machinery, and manure.
-Clean farm implements before entering the groundnut field.
-Avoid allowing weeds to flower and set seed.
-Compost farmyard manure properly before application.
-Keep field borders and bunds weed-free.

2. Cultural Methods
-Use clean and certified groundnut seeds free from weed seeds.
-Follow crop rotation with cereals or pulses to break weed cycles.
-Maintain optimum plant spacing and higher crop population for quick canopy cover.
-Select fast-growing and spreading groundnut varieties for better weed suppression.
-Apply well-decomposed FYM/compost instead of undecomposed manure.
-Practice stale seedbed technique: irrigate field before sowing, allow weeds to germinate, then destroy them before planting.
-Use mulching with crop residues or organic mulch to suppress weed emergence.
-Ensure timely sowing to give crop advantage over weeds.
-Adopt proper nutrient management; apply fertilizers near crop rows to favour crop growth.
-Maintain field sanitation by removing weeds from bunds and irrigation channels.

3. Mechanical / Physical Methods
-Perform summer ploughing to expose weed seeds and underground propagules.
-Carry out intercultivation/hoe weeding at early crop stages.
-Conduct hand weeding at critical stages (around 20–25 DAS and 40–45 DAS).
-Use wheel hoes or tine weeders between rows.
-Remove weeds before flowering and seed formation.
-Use mulches to physically block weed emergence.
 
 4.Chemical Methods (where permitted and recommended)

I. Pre-Sowing Management
-This stage involves treating the soil before the seeds are actually planted to ensure a "clean" seedbed.
-Chemical Treatment: Apply Fluchloralin 45%EC at a rate of 2.0 liters per hectare (l/ha) and for acre  800 ml of chemical .
-Application Method: The herbicide is applied directly to the soil and must be incorporated (mixed) into the top layer of the soil.

II. Pre-Emergence Management
-This treatment occurs after the seeds are sown but before the crop or weeds have emerged from the soil surface.
-Chemical Treatment: Use  Fluchloralin 45%EC at 2.0 l/ha. 800 ml in 360 L of water per acre.
-Application Method: The herbicide should be mixed with 900 liters of water per hectare 
-sprayed using a flat fan nozzle. This nozzle type is preferred because it provides uniform coverage across the soil surface.

--"Post-emergence" means these are applied directly to the foliage after the weeds have already sprouted.
-Imazethapyr 10% SL Target: A broad-spectrum systemic herbicide effective against annual grasses, sedges, and broadleaf weeds.
Dosage: 1.0 - 1.5 liters mixed in 500 - 700 liters of water per hectare. and per acre 400 ml - 600 ml in 200 - 280 L of water needed to spray.
-Timing: Best applied early, when weeds are at the 1-2 leaf stage or approximately 7-14 days after sowing (DAS).

-Irrigation: Following the spray, irrigation is required.
-Supplemental Manual Control: Even with chemical treatment, one hand weeding is recommended between 35 to 40 days after sowing to remove any late-emerging weeds that escaped the herbicide.

--If no chemical herbicides are used, the crop requires intensive manual labor to keep weed populations under control.
-Hoeing and Weeding: Two rounds of manual hand hoeing and weeding are necessary.
-Timing:First round: On the 20th day after sowing. Second round: On the 40th day after sowing.
-Benefit: Hoeing not only removes weeds but also provides soil aeration, which can be beneficial for root growth.

Protocol for herbicide application techniques, equipments and nozzle specifications

--Pre-Emergence Application (Spraying Before Weeds Appear):
-This method is used to treat the soil surface to prevent weed seeds from germinating. Since you are covering the ground rather than specific leaves, you need a different approach.

-Equipment: Use a low-volume sprayer. This can be either a trolley-mounted version for larger areas or a battery-operated knapsack for smaller plots.

-Mist Quality: These sprayers produce small droplets (a fine mist). This fine spray is essential for creating a uniform chemical "blanket" over the soil, ensuring no weed seeds find a gap to grow through.


--Post-Emergence Application (Spraying After Weeds Appear)
When you are spraying weeds that have already sprouted and are visible in your field, your goal is to drench the leaves thoroughly.

-Equipment: Use a lever-operated knapsack sprayer. These sprayers produce large droplets, which are better for sticking to leaves and reducing "drift" (the wind blowing your chemicals onto nearby crops).

-Settings: Use a flat fan or flood jet nozzle. Keep your pressure low—ideally between 15 to 20 psi.

-Technique: Maintain a steady pace by pumping the lever at a speed of 7 to 10 strokes per minute. This ensures a consistent flow of weedicide across the field.

Safety and Precautions:
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) Operators must wear protective clothing, including chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, long-sleeved shirts, long pants, and rubber boots to prevent skin and eye contact.
Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI):  While Pendimethalin is a pre-emergence herbicide and is applied long before harvest, always adhere to the label instructions regarding environmental safety and runoff prevention.
Environmental Safety:  Avoid application during high winds to prevent spray drift into non-target areas or water bodies.

question: What are the effective management strategies and control measures for viral diseases in chilli crops in Madhya Pradesh?
final_answer:
Viral diseases such as Leaf Curl Virus and Mosaic Complex can affect chilli crops and cause symptoms such as leaf curling, mosaic symptoms, stunted growth and reduced fruit size. Their management mainly involves healthy planting material, removal of infected plants, weed management, crop rotation and management of insect vectors.

1. Leaf Curl Virus

Symptoms:
- The disease causes abaxial and adaxial curling of leaves, along with puckering and blistering of the interveinal areas, thickening and swelling of the veins.
- At advanced stages, axillary buds are stimulated, producing clusters of leaves that are reduced in size.
- The whole plant develops a bushy appearance with stunted growth.
- Flowers and fruits are few and small and become curled at the end.
- The disease spreads from plant to plant through the whitefly insect.

Management:

Cultural Management:
- Use healthy planting material and plant only healthy seedlings.
- Regularly monitor the nursery and field for leaf curl symptoms.
- Periodically remove and destroy diseased plants from the nursery and field.
- Remove all weeds from and around the field, as several weeds can act as hosts of the virus.
- Maintain proper field sanitation by removing infected plant material.
- Give particular attention to early detection and removal of infected plants to limit disease spread.

Whitefly (Vector) Management:
- Regularly monitor the whitefly population.
- In case of severe infestation, spray Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 5 g in 15 litres of water.

2. Mosaic Complex

Damage symptoms:
- Symptoms vary depending on the virus, including TMV and CMV.
- Raised blisters and mottled areas of light and dark green appear on the foliage.
- Leaves may point towards the ground.
- Necrotic spots may develop on the stem.
- Fruits ripen unevenly and may be reduced in size.
- There is a reduction in leaf size and narrowing of the lamina, with chlorosis leading to mosaic symptoms.
- Downward curling of leaves may occur along with midrib symptoms.
- Fruits may be small and distorted and may occur on volunteer chilli plants and infected plant debris.

Management:

Cultural control:
- Select healthy seeds for planting.
- Follow crop rotation with non-host crops.
- Control perennial weed hosts.
- Rogue out and destroy infected plants during the early stages of infection.
- Grow disease-tolerant varieties.
- Raise 4 rows of maize or sorghum as a border crop to restrict the spread of aphid vectors.
- Cover the seedbed with nylon net or paddy straw.

Chemical control:
Vector management:
- Treat seeds with Imidacloprid 70% WS @ 10 g/kg seed.
- Apply Fipronil 5% SC @ 320–400 ml in 200 litres of water/acre.

General Safety Precautions for Spraying:
- Use only recommended and approved herbicides for the particular crop and weed.
- Always follow the label/leaflet instructions for dose, dilution, application method and waiting period.
- Wear protective clothing, gloves, mask/respirator, eye protection and footwear while preparing and spraying.
- Do not eat, drink or smoke while handling or spraying herbicides.
- Avoid spraying during strong winds, very hot conditions or when rain is expected.
- Keep children and animals away from the spraying area.
- Avoid contact of the spray solution with the skin, eyes and mouth.
- Do not spray against the wind direction.
- Wash hands, face and exposed body parts thoroughly with soap and clean water after spraying.
- Clean spraying equipment properly after use.
- Dispose of empty containers safely and never reuse them for storing food, water or household materials.

Conclusion:
Effective management of viral diseases in chilli involves using healthy planting material, regular monitoring, removing infected plants, controlling weeds and following suitable cultural practices. Managing insect vectors is also important to restrict the spread of Leaf Curl Virus and Mosaic Complex in chilli crops.

For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

question: What are the recommended nutrient management practices and growth stimulants to improve flowering and blooming in Pigeon Pea?
final_answer:
Pigeon pea (Tur/Redgram) is a leguminous crop capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen through its association with Rhizobium bacteria. To achieve proper pod development, seed filling, and maximum yield, the crop should receive the recommended nutrients at sowing and adequate moisture during the flowering and pod-filling stages.

Basal Fertilizer Application

1.For Sole Pigeon Pea (Tur)
Apply 10 kg Nitrogen and 20 kg Phosphorus per acre at the time of sowing.
This can be supplied through 50 kg DAP per acre.

2.For Drought-Prone Areas
Apply 25 kg Nitrogen/ha (approximately 10 kg/acre) and 25 kg Phosphorus/ha (approximately 10 kg/acre) through chemical fertilizers at sowing.

Fertilizer equivalent:
Urea: 54 kg/ha (approximately 22 kg/acre) to supply 25 kg N.
SSP: 156 kg/ha (approximately 63 kg/acre) to supply 25 kg P₂O₅.

Apart from proper nutrient management, the following cultivation practices are essential for achieving healthy growth and higher yields in pigeon pea. 

Seed Treatment
-Treat seed with Rhizobium and Phosphorus Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) @ 25 g/kg seed each.
-For a seed rate of 12–15 kg/ha (4.9–6.1 kg/acre), approximately 125–153 g each of Rhizobium and PSB per acre is required.

Organic Nutrient Management
-Incorporate 1 tonne of well-decomposed press mud per hectare one month before sowing to supply an additional 20 kg N and 20 kg P₂O₅ per hectare (8 kg N and 8 kg P₂O₅ per acre).

Micronutrient Management
-If symptoms such as yellowing between veins on older leaves or stunted plant growth appear, apply Zinc Sulphate @ 10 kg/ha (4 kg/acre) along with Manganese Sulphate @ 5 kg/ha (2 kg/acre) at the time of sowing.

Application Method
-Dissolve the micronutrients in about 200 litres of water per hectare (about 80 litres per acre).
-Spray uniformly over the crop using a knapsack sprayer fitted with a flat fan nozzle.
-Repeat the spray after 15 days if necessary.

Growth Regulator Application
To improve flowering and blooming, apply any one of the following growth regulators:

1. Gibberellic Acid (GA₃): Apply 100 mg GA₃ per litre of water.
-Prepare a solution by dissolving 10 g GA₃ in 1 litre of water.
-Use this solution for spraying.

2. Ethephon 39% SL: Apply 1 ml EtOH₃9% SL per litre of water.
-Prepare a solution by dissolbing 10 ml EtOH₃9% SL in 1 litre of water.
-Use this solution as a foliar spray.

Safety Precautions
-Wear gloves, mask, protective clothing, and eye protection while handling and applying growth regulators.
-Avoid direct contact with skin and eyes.
-Follow the manufacturer's label instructions regarding dosage and application method.
-Do not exceed the recommended concentration.
-Store growth regulators safely away from food, feed, children, livestock, and pets.

Conclusion
Achieving good flowering and pod formation in pigeon pea depends on supplying the recommended dose of nitrogen and phosphorus at sowing, maintaining adequate soil moisture during flowering and pod development, and ensuring balanced nutrition throughout the crop period. The use of Rhizobium and PSB biofertilizers, organic manures, zinc sulphate, manganese sulphate, and appropriate growth regulators helps improve flowering, pod setting, and overall productivity.

question: How to control Powdery Mildew in Chilli in Andhra Pradesh?
final_answer:
Powdery mildew is an important fungal disease of chilli caused by Leveillula taurica. The disease appears as white powdery growth on leaves, which gradually spreads to branches and young fruits, resulting in premature defoliation, poor fruit development, and significant yield loss if not managed at the early stage.

Symptoms:
- White powdery coating appears mostly on the lower surface and occasionally on the upper surface.
- Correspondingly, on the upper surface, yellow patches are seen.
- Severe infection results in the drying and shedding of affected leaves.
- Powdery growth can also be seen on branches and young fruits.
- Diseased fruits do not grow further and may drop prematurely.

Survival and spread:
Primary: Dormant mycelium in infected crop debris
Secondary: Wind-dispersed conidia

Favourable conditions:
Cool, dry weather favours conidial germination
High RH favours disease development

Management:
Cultural control:
Use healthy, certified, and weed-free seeds.
Avoid planting overlapping crops in adjacent areas.
In the nursery, all infected plants should be carefully removed and destroyed.
Grow resistant varieties like Phule Mukta.

Chemical control:
Spray any one of the following:
Hexaconazole 2% SC @ 10 ml mixed in 10 litres of water/acre or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 10 ml mixed in 10 litres water/acre or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 200 ml mixed in 200–300 litres of water/acre or Propiconazole 25% EC @ 200 ml mixed in 20–24 litres of water/acre or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 600 g mixed in 300 litres of water/acre or Zineb 75% WP @ 600–800 g mixed in 300–400 litres of water/acre or Sulphur 80% WP @ 1 kg mixed in 300–400 litres water/acre or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 100 g mixed in 200 litres of water/acre or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 200 g mixed in 200 litres of Water/acre or Hexaconazole 5% EC @ 200 ml mixed in about 200 litres of water/acre or Propiconazole + Hexaconazole 75% WG @ 100 g mixed in 20–24 litres of water per acre or Trifloxystrobin + Tebuconazole 75% WG @ 120 g mixed in 200 litres of water per acre or Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole 325 SC @ 200 ml mixed in 240 litres of water per acre or Azoxystroxin + Pyraclostrobin 133 SC @ 200 ml mixed in 250 litres of water per acre or Azoxystroin + Epoxiconazole 18.3 SE @ 200 ml mixed in 20 litres of water per acre or Azoxystroix + Trifloxystrobin 133 SC @ 20 ml mixed in 200 litres of water per acre.

Conclusion:
Early detection and timely application of recommended fungicides help reduce disease severity and minimize yield losses. Integrated disease management involving cultural practices, seed treatment, balanced nutrition, and need-based fungicide application provides effective protection against powdery mildew in chilli cultivation.

For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

question: What preventive measures can be taken against Dwarf disease (Bona Rog) in paddy crop?
final_answer:
Dwarf disease (Bona Rog) in paddy is caused by Southern rice black-streaked dwarf virus (SRBSDV), which is transmitted by the white-backed planthopper. Since it is a viral disease, no curative treatment is available; therefore, management should focus on preventive measures.

Symptoms:
-Plants show severe stunting or dwarfing and do not grow normally even after recommended fertilizer application.
-In severe cases, infected plants remain only one-third to half or two-thirds of their normal height.
-Leaves become short, dark green and stiff.
-Roots remain shallow, and plants can be easily uprooted.
-Affected plants often wither, show poor panicle emergence, and produce mostly unfilled grains, causing heavy yield loss.

Preventive Management Practices:

Since the causative agent is a virus, direct chemical control against the virus itself is not recommended. Instead, farmers must control the vector insect, the White backed planthopper (WBPH), which transmits the disease.

Field Sanitation
Keep bunds and irrigation channels free from weeds.
Remove infected stunted plants immediately.
Destroy infected plants by deep burial.

Sowing Adjustments: Avoid very early sowing, as stunting symptoms are significantly more pronounced in early-sown paddy crops compared to late-sown ones.

Nursery Level Monitoring: Regularly monitor the rice crop right from the nursery stage onwards specifically for the presence of WBPH.

Field Tapping Method: To check for insects, slightly tilt a few plants and tap their bases 2–3 times. Look closely to see if WBPH adults or nymphs drop and float on the water surface.

Vector Chemical Control: If WBPH is detected, immediately spray any one of the following insecticides mixed in 100 litres of water per acre:
Fipronil 5% SC @ 400 ml/acre
Imidacloprid 70% WG @ 60 g/acre

Alternatively, you may use:
Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 40 g/acre
Flonicamid 50% WG @ 80 g/acre
Spinosad 45% SC @ 60 ml/acre

Spray uniformly over the field ensuring thorough coverage of both upper and lower leaf surfaces where WBPH nymphs and adults usually congregate.

Safety Precautions:
Wear gloves, mask, protective clothing, and eye protection while handling pesticides.
Avoid spraying during strong winds or before rainfall.
Do not eat, drink, or smoke while mixing or applying chemicals.
Follow label instructions regarding dosage, waiting period, and safety precautions.

Conclusion:
Dwarf disease (Bona Rog) cannot be cured once infection occurs because it is a viral disease. Therefore, prevention through timely removal of infected plants, regular monitoring of the crop, maintaining clean fields, and controlling the white-backed planthopper (WBPH) using recommended insecticides are essential. Early detection and rapid action help reduce disease spread and minimize yield losses.

For specific recommendations or field-level diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

question: The farmer needs information regarding the control of Bacterial Leaf Blight in Pea crop
final_answer: Bacterial leaf blight in pea starts with small water-soaked spots on leaves that quickly turn brown, forming irregular patches with yellow edges, and in severe cases, leaves dry up and fall. To manage it, farmers should avoid overhead irrigation, use clean, disease-free seeds, follow crop rotation, remove infected plants, and avoid working in the field when foliage is wet. For chemical control, seed treatment with certified bactericides like copper oxychloride helps in reducing infection, and spraying copper-based fungicides at early stages can slow disease spread, always following recommended doses and intervals for safe use.

question: What are the fertilizers required for Gingelly for top dressing?
final_answer: In gingelly (sesame) cultivation, nutrient management mainly focuses on basal application rather than top dressing. The full recommended dose of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) is applied at the time of sowing. Under rainfed conditions, a basal dose of 9:5:5 kg NPK/acre is recommended, which can be reduced to 7:5:5 kg NPK/acre when supplemented with biofertilizers like Azospirillum and Phosphobacteria. For irrigated conditions, the recommended dose is 14:9:9 kg NPK/acre, which can be reduced to 8:9:9 kg NPK/acre with the use of the same biofertilizers. In addition, 2 kg of manganese sulphate per acre is applied basally to prevent micronutrient deficiency; if interveinal chlorosis appears later, manganese sulphate or zinc sulphate at 2 kg/acre mixed with soil can be broadcasted. Furthermore, TNAU micronutrient (MN) mixture is applied as enriched FYM at 3 kg/acre for rainfed and 5 kg/acre for irrigated sesame, ensuring balanced nutrition and better crop growth.

question: My potato crop has sustained physical damage due to hailstones, and the ambient temperature has dropped significantly. What fertilizers or management practices should I implement to mitigate damage and protect the crop in Madhya Pradesh?
final_answer:
Hail damage and frost are common weather-related stresses that can significantly impact potato crops, particularly during the early growth stages. These events cause physical injury to leaves, stems, and tubers, leading to reduced photosynthesis, nutrient uptake, and overall plant vigor.
 
Understanding Hail Damage in Potatoes:
Hailstones can cause direct mechanical injury by tearing foliage, breaking tender shoots, and damaging young tubers. The severity of damage depends on the size and frequency of hailstorms. In Madhya Pradesh's Chhindwara district, where temperatures often drop below freezing after heavy rainfall or snowfall, combined with hail impacts, plants may experience both immediate physiological stress and delayed recovery.
 
Immediate Management After Hailstorm:
1. Assess Crop Damage: Inspect fields for broken stems, leaf injuries, and damaged tubers. Remove severely injured plants immediately to prevent secondary infections from pathogens like Phytophthora blight.
2. Provide Light Irrigation: If soil moisture is low due to hail-induced runoff, give a light irrigation (about 5 cm) to restore water balance and support plant recovery.
3. Protect Remaining Plants: Cover remaining healthy plants with straw mulch or crop residues to protect them from further wind and temperature fluctuations.
4. Prevent Secondary Infections: Apply a protective fungicide spray if hail has caused wounds on stems or leaves. Use copper-based fungicides at recommended doses.

Nutrient Management Considerations:
Potato requires balanced nutrition throughout its growth cycle, but extreme weather conditions require special attention to ensure proper recovery.
 
Fertilizer Application Recommendations:
For Madhya Pradesh's Chhindwara region, apply fertilizers based on soil test results. However, as a general guideline:
- Nitrogen (N): 60 kg/acre (Kufri Jyoti), 80 kg/acre (Kufri Pukhraj)
- Phosphorus (P₂O₅): 20 kg/acre
- Potash (K₂O): 20 kg/acre

Apply full phosphorus and potash along with half nitrogen at sowing. Apply the remaining nitrogen in two equal splits: first top-dressing at 30 days after planting and second top-dressing at 45–50 days after planting. This split application helps maintain adequate vegetative growth while supporting tuber development under adverse weather conditions.
 
Organic Matter Addition:
Incorporate well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM) or compost into the soil before planting. Organic matter improves soil structure, increases microbial activity, and enhances drought tolerance. Apply FYM @ 25 t/ha (10 t/acre) before final land preparation.
 
Soil Moisture Conservation:
Maintain optimal soil moisture through regular irrigation. Avoid prolonged dry spells after hailstorms because potatoes have shallow root systems and cannot tolerate extended periods without water. Ensure good drainage to prevent waterlogging, which can exacerbate frost damage.
 
Safety Precautions During Fertilizer Application:
When handling chemical fertilizers, wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE):
- Chemical-resistant gloves
- Face mask or respirator
- Protective clothing including long-sleeved shirts and pants
- Eye protection such as goggles or face shield
 
Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI):
If you plan to harvest within 7–10 days after applying any foliar sprays, follow the PHI strictly. For most commonly used pesticides, this period ranges from 7–14 days depending on the product.
 
Harvesting Strategy:
Harvest potatoes when tubers reach marketable size and skin color changes from greenish to brown. Delayed harvesting can lead to increased susceptibility to diseases like scab and rotting. Harvest only matured tubers; immature ones should be left in the field until they develop sufficient strength.
 
Monitoring and Follow-Up:
Continue monitoring the crop for signs of disease infection, especially bacterial wilt, which thrives in cool, wet conditions. Maintain field sanitation by removing infected plant debris and ensuring proper drainage channels remain unobstructed.
 
For specific recommendations tailored to your local conditions, soil type, and variety selection, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) in Chhindwara district or consult with agricultural extension officers.

question: What are the symptoms of fertilizer-induced disorders in pea crops, and how can they be managed in MP?
final_answer:
Fertilizer-induced disorders in pea crops occur when nutrients are supplied in deficient, excessive or imbalanced amounts. Excess fertilizer can cause fertilizer or salt injury, while nutrient deficiencies produce characteristic symptoms such as chlorosis, poor growth, reduced pod filling and poor seed development. In Madhya Pradesh, balanced nutrient management based on soil testing and variety-specific requirements helps prevent and manage these disorders.

Fertilizer Recommendation
-Apply fertilizers according to soil-test results and the nutrient requirement of the particular pea variety.

 Tall variety:
-Nitrogen: 20 kg/ha (8.09 kg/acre) → Urea 43.5 kg/ha (17.6 kg/acre)
-Phosphorus: 40 kg P₂O₅/ha (16.19 kg/acre) → SSP 250 kg/ha (101 kg/acre)
-Potassium: 40 kg K₂O/ha (16.19 kg/acre) → MOP 67 kg/ha (27 kg/acre)
-Sulphur: 20 kg/ha (8.09 kg/acre)

Dwarf variety:
-Nitrogen: 20 kg/ha (8.09 kg/acre) → Urea 43.5 kg/ha (17.6 kg/acre)
-Phosphorus: 50 kg P₂O₅/ha (20.23 kg/acre) → SSP 313 kg/ha (127 kg/acre)
-Potassium: 50 kg K₂O/ha (20.23 kg/acre) → MOP 83 kg/ha (34 kg/acre)
-Sulphur: 20 kg/ha (8.09 kg/acre)

Major nutrient deficiencies in pea and their management include:

1. Nitrogen Deficiency
Symptoms:
-General yellowing and light green colour of the plant.
-Stunted growth and small leaves.
-Symptoms appear first on older, lower leaves.
-Lower leaves gradually turn pale yellow to yellow, followed by white and brown necrotic areas under severe deficiency.

Management:
-Apply 20 kg N/ha (8.09 kg/acre) for both varieties.
-This corresponds to approximately 43.5 kg urea/ha (17.6 kg/acre).

2. Potassium Deficiency
Symptoms:
-Lower leaves become dark green initially, followed by yellowing and marginal chlorosis.
-Leaflets may curl or cup downward.
-Plant growth is retarded.
-Pods may be poorly filled.

Management:
-High-altitude variety: 40 kg K₂O/ha (16.19 kg/acre).
-Bonnie variety: 50 kg K₂O/ha (20.23 kg/acre).
-Equivalent MOP requirement is approximately 67 kg/ha (27 kg/acre) and 83 kg/ha (34 kg/acre), respectively.

3. Sulphur Deficiency
Symptoms:
-Younger leaves, including the veins, turn yellow.
-Severe deficiency may cause yellowing of older leaves.
-Plants remain small and slender.

Management:
-Apply 20 kg S/ha (8.09 kg/acre) for both varieties based on soil-test recommendations.

4. Iron Deficiency
Symptoms:
-Yellowing occurs between the leaf veins.
-Leaves may become severely chlorotic due to reduced chlorophyll.
-High-pH black clay soils may predispose pea to iron and manganese deficiencies.

Management:
-Where iron deficiency is confirmed, apply 0.1% ferrous sulphate (1 g/L water) as a foliar spray.

5. Zinc Deficiency
Symptoms:
-Leaves become narrow, pointed and inwardly curled.
-Yellow mottling develops on the leaf lamina, beginning near the base of the midrib.
-Poor pod setting and seed development may occur.

Management:
-Apply zinc sulphate @ 15 kg/ha (6 kg/acre).

6. Boron Deficiency
Symptoms:
-Stems become thickened and stiff.
-Plants develop a short, squat and bushy appearance.
-Foliage becomes chlorotic.
-Young leaflets remain small and leaf tips may turn brown.
-Growing points may die.

Management:
-Apply boron 20% @ 1–2 g/L water as a foliar spray.

7. Magnesium Deficiency
Symptoms:
-Older leaves develop characteristic interveinal chlorosis.
-Areas between the veins lose their green colour while veins remain green.
-In pea, central interveinal chlorosis with a green marginal band may occur.

Management:
-Spray 0.5% MgSO₄ (5 g/L water) + 1% urea (10 g/L water).
-Apply MgSO₄ @ 25–50 kg/ha (10–20 kg/acre) through the soil where required.

8. Manganese Deficiency
Symptoms:
-Young leaves become yellow to white while veins remain green.
-A characteristic grey-speck symptom may appear.
-New leaves progressively become more chlorotic.
-Brown lesions may occur in the centre of cotyledons, associated with Marsh spot in pea seeds.

Management:
-Spray 0.5% MnSO₄ (5 g/L water).
-Apply manganese sulphate @ 25 kg/ha (10 kg/acre) through the soil where deficiency is confirmed.

Fertilizer Injury and Nutrient Imbalance
-Avoid excessive or repeated fertilizer application because it may cause salt injury, fertilizer burn and nutrient imbalance.
-Follow soil-test-based fertilizer recommendations.
-Maintain adequate soil moisture and proper drainage.
-Apply micronutrients only when deficiency is confirmed.
-Avoid indiscriminate mixing of fertilizers and foliar nutrients.
-Use recommended concentrations for foliar applications.
-Avoid applying foliar nutrients during very hot or unsuitable weather conditions.

Safety Precautions
-Wear gloves, mask and protective clothing during fertilizer and chemical application.
-Follow recommended doses and label instructions.
-Avoid spraying during strong winds or when rainfall is expected.
-Prefer morning or evening application under suitable weather conditions.
-Maintain the prescribed pre-harvest interval (PHI) wherever pesticides are used.
-Avoid applying fertilizers, micronutrients or pesticides at excessive concentrations, as this can cause additional crop injury.

Conclusion
Balanced and soil-test-based nutrient management is essential for preventing fertilizer-induced disorders in pea. Proper application of N, P, K and S, along with targeted correction of confirmed micronutrient deficiencies, helps maintain healthy growth, pod formation and seed development. For location-specific diagnosis and recommendations in Madhya Pradesh, farmers can consult their nearest KVK or Block Agriculture Officer

For further guidance and location-specific recommendations, farmers are advised to contact their nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

question: What is the role of a growth regulator in the cultivation of Jasmine, and how can it be effectively used for Celosia?
final_answer:
Growth regulators are plant hormones that regulate various physiological processes in plants, including cell division, differentiation, and growth. In Jasmine cultivation, they play a crucial role in promoting healthy vegetative growth, improving flowering, enhancing fruit set, and increasing yield.

Role of Growth Regulators in Jasmine Cultivation:

1. Gibberellic Acid (GA₃): 
- Promotes stem elongation and branching.
- Enhances vegetative growth and overall plant vigor.
- Improves flowering and fruit development when applied at the appropriate stage.

2. Naphthalene Acetic Acid (NAA):
- Stimulates root initiation and promotes rooting of cuttings.
- Enhances vegetative growth and improves plant establishment.

3. Ethephon 39% SL:
- Induces flower bud formation and enhances flowering.
- Increases fruit set and improves crop productivity.

4. Triacontanol 0.05% EC:
- Promotes vigorous vegetative growth and improves plant health.
- Enhances nutrient uptake and supports better crop performance.

Application Methods for Jasmine:

For Jasmine cultivation, growth regulators should be applied as foliar sprays using clean water. The recommended doses vary depending on the specific hormone being used and the stage of plant growth.

Recommended Doses:

1. Gibberellic Acid (GA₅) @ 10–20 ppm: Apply 1 ml per litre of water during the early stages of vegetative growth to promote strong stem development and branching.

2. Naphthalene Acetic Acid (NAK) @ 100 ppm: Spray 1 ml per litre of water during the active vegetative phase to enhance root initiation and improve plant establishment.

3. Ethephon 39 % SL @ 100 ppm: Apply 1 ml per litre of water at the pre-flowering stage to induce flower bud formation and increase fruit set.

4. Triacontanol 0.005% EC @ 100 ppm: Spray 1 ml mixed with 1 kg of sand or soil per square meter during the vegetative growth period to promote vigorous vegetative growth and improve plant vigor.

Safety Precautions:

When handling and applying growth regulators, farmers must wear protective gloves, masks, goggles, and full-sleeved clothing to prevent skin contact and inhalation. Avoid spraying during windy conditions to minimize drift. Store growth regulators in their original containers away from food items and out of reach of children.

Conclusion:

Effective use of growth regulators in jasmine cultivation can significantly improve vegetative growth, flowering, fruit set, and overall yield. By following the recommended dosages and application methods, farmers can optimize plant physiology and achieve better crop performance.

For field-specific recommendations or diagnosis, please contact your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or Block Agriculture Officer.

question: How can I identify and manage fungal infections and Iron (Fe) deficiency in my Tapioca crop in Kerala?
final_answer:
Tapioca (Manihot esculenta) is susceptible to several fungal pathogens that can significantly reduce tuber yield and quality. While iron is an essential micronutrient for tapioca crop growth. It plays a vital role in chlorophyll formation, photosynthesis, and overall plant development. Adequate iron nutrition helps maintain healthy green foliage and supports proper crop growth. When iron is deficient, the plant's ability to produce chlorophyll is reduced, resulting in poor growth and reduced productivity.

Major Fungal Diseases and Their Management:

1. Tuber rot Symptoms:
The initial symptoms are leaves turning brown and wilting.
The leaves may remain attached to the plant or drop to the ground.
The infected plant will show a scorched appearance.
The examination of roots reveals root dieback and swelling of tubers.
Tubers may have light brown, dark gray, blue or pink discoloration.
The rotting roots may be soft and produce a foul odor.
In some cases, white fungal structures can be seen at the base of the stem, particularly during the wet season.

Management: 
Provide good drainage facilities.
Removal of infected tubers
Deep ploughing with chisel plough
Ridge planting
Apply Trichoderma viride (1 kg/acre) as basal and at 3rd and 6th month after planting to soil.
In case of Severe Infestation, spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2 g per litre of water (for one acre spray 400 g in 200 litres of water). 

2. Anthracnose 
Symptoms:
Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, stems, flowers, and fruits.
The affected leaves wilt and droop downwards.
Wilted leaves later fall from the plant.
Cankers can be seen on stems and leaf petioles.
Death of shoots or die back occurs.
Soft parts of plant become necrotic, twisted and distorted.

Management:
Do not wet the foliage while irrigation.
The diseased twigs should be pruned and burnt along with fallen leaves.
Remove and destroy infected crop debris.
For severe infestation, spray either Mancozeb 75% WP @ 3 g per litre of water (for one acre 600 g in 200 litres of water), or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 2 g per litre of water (400 g per acre in 200 litres of water). 
Treat stem cuttings or apply Trichoderma harzianum or Trichoderma viride around the root zone/soil to suppress fungal pathogens.
Apply Pseudomonas fluorescens as a foliar spray or soil application, where recommended, to reduce disease incidence.

3. Leaf Spot
Symptoms:
The symptoms of the disease appear on the leaves as small brown coloured
necrotic spots surrounded by yellow halo
The size, shape, colour and form of the leaf spot vary in accordance with the
causal organisms.
Spots are produced on both the sides of leaves.
On upper surface brown spots with dark border appears.
On lower side of the leaf spots with grey centre and less distinct margin appear.
In some cases white spots are also seen on upper surface.
The infected leaves turn yellow and dry up

Management:
Field sanitation
Crop rotation
Use resistant varieties like S-856, H-97 and Sree Visakham.
Avoid working in the field when foliage is wet to minimize the spread of fungal spores.
Disinfect pruning tools before moving between plants.
For severe infestation, spray either Mancozeb 75% WP @ 3 g per litre of water (for one acre 600 g in 200 litres of water), or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2 g per litre of water (400 g per acre in 200 litres of water). 
Apply Trichoderma harzianum or Trichoderma viride as a soil application or for stem cutting treatment to suppress fungal pathogens.
Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens on the foliage (where recommended) to help reduce leaf spot incidence.

Safety and Precautions:
 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Always wear gloves, masks, goggles, and protective clothing when handling and spraying chemical fungicides.


Iron Deficiency and Management: 
Farmers can identify iron deficiency in tapioca by observing the following symptoms:

Symptoms of Iron Deficiency
Deficient plants exhibit interveinal chlorosis, where the tissue between the veins becomes yellow while the veins remain green.
Green veins become prominent against the yellowish interveinal areas.
White or yellowish new leaves are formed due to severe deficiency.
Leaf size is reduced.
Wilting of leaves may occur.
Delayed maturation of the crop is observed.
Stunted growth of plants is common.

Farmers are advised to adopt the following recommendations to manage iron deficiency:

Management Recommendations:
Conduct a soil test to determine the actual cause of the problem, as iron content in some soils may already be high.
Maintain balanced nutrient management, as low potassium levels can lead to iron deficiency.
Apply Ferrous Sulphate @ 60 g per plant (or 6 kg per acre) to deficient soils.

question: What to do after accidental spraying of wrong herbicide?
final_answer:
Accidental application of wrong herbicide on paddy crop can cause significant phytotoxicity and stress to the plants. However, immediate corrective measures can help minimize the damage and support crop recovery.
 
Immediate Action - Neutralization Treatment:
The most effective immediate remedy is to spray a solution of slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) to neutralize the herbicide effects. Prepare a solution by dissolving 2.5 grams of slaked lime per liter of water. Apply this solution uniformly across the affected paddy field as soon as possible after the wrong herbicide application. This lime solution helps neutralize acidic herbicide residues and reduces their toxic effects on the crop.
 
Follow-up Nutrient Management:
After the lime application, the crop will need nutritional support to recover from the stress. Conduct a soil test to assess nutrient status and pH levels. Apply well-decomposed Farm Yard Manure (FYM) at 4 to 4.8 tonnes per acre or vermicompost at 2 to 2.4 tonnes per acre to improve soil health and provide organic nutrition. These organic amendments help in detoxification and improve soil microbial activity.
 
NPK and Micronutrient Support:
Provide a foliar spray of NPK (19:19:19) at 5 to 10 grams per liter of water. This helps the crop recover quickly by providing readily available nutrients through leaves. 

Additional Recovery Measures:
 1. Ensure adequate irrigation to dilute and leach out herbicide residues from the root zone
 2. Avoid any additional chemical applications for at least 10-15 days
 3. Apply bio-stimulants or seaweed extracts (2-3 ml per liter) to promote plant growth and stress recovery
 4. Monitor the crop daily for signs of recovery or further deterioration
 5. Maintain proper water level in paddy fields (2-3 inches) to reduce herbicide uptake
 
Protective Gear for Chemical Applications:
When handling slaked lime or any chemical fertilizers, wear chemical-resistant gloves, face mask, protective clothing with long sleeves and full pants, and eye protection. Wash hands thoroughly after application and store all chemicals away from children, animals, and food items.
 
Safety Guidelines:
Follow recommended doses strictly for all corrective treatments. Ensure proper application timing and avoid mixing different chemicals unless specifically recommended. Dispose of empty containers properly and maintain emergency contact numbers for immediate assistance.
 
The recovery process may take 2-3 weeks depending on the severity of herbicide damage. Patience and consistent care are essential for crop recuperation.
 
For further guidance or clarification, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

question: What are the uses of Fenvalerate in paddy cultivation?
final_answer:
Fenvalerate is a synthetic pyrethroid insecticide widely used in paddy cultivation to control various pests, particularly stem borers and leaf folders. It acts as an effective contact and stomach poison against these major rice pests.
 
Target Pests:
- Stem Borer: The larvae bore into the stem, causing dead hearts (white earheads) during the tillering stage.
- Leaf Folder: Caterpillars fold leaves longitudinally and feed on the green tissue, reducing photosynthesis and grain filling.
 
Recommended Dose and Application Method:
For paddy crops, Fenvalerate 20% EC should be applied at a dose of 150 ml per acre mixed in 200 liters of water. This formulation provides excellent coverage for both early and late-stage infestations. Apply when pest populations reach economic threshold levels or show visible damage symptoms.
 
Application Timing:
The best time for application is during evening hours (6 PM - 8 PM) when temperatures are moderate and wind speed is low. Avoid spraying during peak sunlight hours to prevent phytotoxicity and ensure better efficacy.
 
Safety Precautions:
Wear protective clothing including gloves, mask, long-sleeved shirts, full pants, and closed footwear while handling pesticides. Do not eat, drink, or smoke during mixing and spraying operations. Wash hands thoroughly with soap after application. Store pesticides in original containers away from children, animals, food items, and drinking water sources. Dispose of empty containers safely by puncturing them and burying them away from water bodies.
 
Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI):
Maintain a minimum PHI of 3 days before harvesting the crop to ensure chemical residues are within safe limits for consumption.
 
Monitoring and Follow-Up:
Regularly monitor fields for new infestations using light traps or pheromone traps. If pest pressure persists despite one spray, consider additional applications based on local agricultural advisories.
 
For further guidance or clarification, farmers are advised to contact the nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or local agricultural extension officer.

question: How can I control Dila weed in maize in Rupnagar?
final_answer:
Dila is a sedge weed commonly known as nutgrass. Its scientific name is Cyperus rotundus, and it belongs to the Cyperaceae family. It is a perennial weed that spreads mainly through underground tubers and rhizomes and can compete strongly with crops for water, nutrients, light and space.

(A) Preventive and cultural control:
- Use certified seeds or 'Clean seed' from a known source free from admixture of weed seeds.
- Cleaning seeds by dipping in 2% brine solution helps in separation of floating weed seeds.
- Avoid application of undecomposed farmyard manure as it contains viable weed seeds.
- Off-season ploughing after rice harvest reduces weed seed replenishment.
- Go for deep summer ploughing during April-May to expose the vegetative propagules of certain weeds and also to bury the weed seeds at a depth that prevents germination.
- Interculture with a Paddy Weeder, 15 days after transplanting and again after a fortnight. Where a paddy weeder cannot be run, hand weeding may be done.

(B) Chemical control:
(i) Pre-emergence herbicides:
- Any of the herbicides given below may be applied by mixing with 60 kg of sand per acre in standing water within 2 to 3 days of transplanting.
- Spray Butachlor 50 EC @ 1200 ml/acre or Butachlor 50 EW @ 1200 ml or Anilofos 18 EC @ 850 ml/acre or Anilofos 30 EC @ 500 ml/acre or Pendimethalin 30 EC @ 1000 to 1200 ml/acre or Pretilachlor 50 EC @ 600 ml/acre or Pretilachlor 37.5 WG @ 400 g/acre or Pyrazosulfuron ethyl 10 WP @ 100 g/acre or Metsulfuron methyl 20 SG @ 10 g/acre or Bispyribac sodium 10 SC @ 100 ml/acre or Bispyribac sodium 38 DF @ 100 g/acre or Clodinafop-propargyl 15 WP @ 400 g/acre or Fenoxaprop-p-ethyl 9.3 EC @ 400 ml/acre or Quizalofop-ethyl 5 EC @ 400 ml/acre or Quizralophen 10 EC @ 400 ml/acre or Sulfosulfuron 75 WG @ 10 g/acre or Carfentrazone ethyl 40 DF @ 100 g/acre or Carfentrazone ethy 40 DF @ 100 g/ acre or Metribuzin 70 WP @ 200 g/acre or Metribuzin 70 WP @ 100 g/acre or Metribuzin 50 WP @ 200 g/acre or Pyrithiobac sodium 10 EC @ 400 ml/ acre or Pyrithiobac sodium 6 % + Chlorimuron ethyl 3 % WDG @ 200 g/acre or Pyrhiobac sodium 10 EC @ 40 ml/acre or Pyrhiobac sodium 15 EC @ 200 ml/acre or Pyrhiobac sodium + Metsulfuron methyl 10 SE @ 100 ml/acre or Pyrhiobac Sodium + Chlorimuron Ethyl 38 DF @ 100 g/ acre or Pyrhiobac Sodium + ChlorimuronEthyl 38 DF @ 100 g /acre or Pyrhiobac Sodium + Metsulfuron Methyl 10 SE @ 100 ml/ acre or Pyrhiobac Sodium + Chloridazon 38 DF @ 100 g/ acer or Pyrhiobac Sodium + Chloridazon + Metsulfuron Methyl 10 SE @100 ml/acre or Pyrhiobax Sodium + Chloridazon + Metsulfuron Methyl10 SE @ 100 ml/acre

(ii) Post emergence herbicide:
- Apply any one of the following post-emergence herbicides when weeds are at 2–4 leaf stage (about 20–25 DAS).
- Pendimethalin 30 EC @ 1.0 L/acre
- Metsulfuron methyl 20 WG @ 10 g/acre
- Bispyribac-sodium 10% w/w @ 100 ml/acre
- Quizalofop-ethyl 5% EC @ 400 ml/acre
- Quizalofop-p-ethyl 10% EC @ 400 ml/acre
Apply these herbicides using 200 litres of water per acre.

(C) Mechanical control:
- Hand weeding should be carried out at 20–25 DAS if required.

(D) Biological control:
- Conserve natural enemies such as ants, spiders, beetles, birds, etc., which help suppress weed populations naturally.

question: What are the key differences between Basmati and non-Basmati paddy varieties, and how should I choose the right variety for my farm in Andhra Pradesh?
final_answer:
Basmati rice is a premium aromatic long-grain rice known for its extra-long, slender grains, which elongate to at least twice their original length after cooking. It has a soft, fluffy texture, a superior aroma, a distinct flavour, and excellent cooking qualities. These unique characteristics are influenced by the agro-climatic conditions of the Himalayan foothill region, along with proper harvesting, processing, and ageing practices.

Non-Basmati rice refers to all rice varieties other than Basmati. It includes short-, medium-, and long-grain rice that may be aromatic or non-aromatic, with varying cooking qualities and textures. Unlike Basmati, which is known for its distinctive aroma and long grain elongation after cooking, non-Basmati rice is primarily valued for its adaptability, high yield, and suitability for diverse agro-climatic conditions. It is widely cultivated across India and is used for daily consumption, processed foods, and exports. Varieties such as Sona Masuri, Swarna, IR64, Samba Mahsuri, and the OUAT Kalinga Rice series are examples of non-Basmati rice.

Some basmati and non-basmati varieties are : 

. CSR 30 (Basmati type) 
-Plant height: ~155 cm 
-Maturity: ~155 days 
-Grain type: Extra-long slender (Basmati type) 
Salt tolerance: -Sodicity up to pH ~9.5 -Salinity up to ~7.0 dS/m 
Yield: -Normal soils: ~3.0 t/ha (10 q/acre) 
-Salt-affected soils: ~2.0 t/ha (8q/acre)
 Special features: 
-First salt-tolerant variety released from CSRI 
-Resistant to blast disease 
-Has good resistance to bacterial leaf blight

Pusa Basmati 1847 (2024) is a semi-dwarf variety with a plant height of about 108 cm. It produces extra-long, slender grains that are soft, non-sticky, and almost double in length after cooking. The variety matures in about 99 days after transplanting and gives an average yield of 19.0 quintals per acre. It is resistant to all ten pathotypes of bacterial blight prevalent in Punjab and shows moderate resistance to neck blast.

Punjab Basmati 7 (2021) is a semi-dwarf variety about 111 cm tall with extra-long, slender grains that are soft, non-stick, and elongate well on cooking. It is highly aromatic, similar to traditional Basmati types. The variety matures in around 101 days after transplanting, yields about 19.0 quintals per acre, and is resistant to all ten prevalent pathotypes of bacterial blight in Punjab.

Pusa Basmati 1718 (2019) is an improved, bacterial blight–resistant version of Pusa Basmati 1121, resistant to all ten prevalent pathotypes in Punjab. It has an average plant height of 121 cm, matures in about 114 days after transplanting, and bears extra-long, slender grains with good cooking quality. The average yield is 17.0 quintals per acre.

Punjab Basmati 5 (2017) is a semi-dwarf variety with a height of about 112 cm. It produces extra-long, slender grains with excellent cooking and eating quality; the grains are non-sticky, highly aromatic, and nearly double in length after cooking. The variety matures in about one hundred days after transplanting and gives an average yield of 20.0 quintals per acre. It is resistant to bacterial leaf blight and moderately resistant to stem borer.

IR 64 (1964) is a dwarf variety with a plant height of about 100 cm. It produces medium-long, slender grains that are slightly sticky but have good cooking quality. question: What is the recommended method for applying fertilizers to promote flower development in cotton in Karnataka?
final_answer:
To promote better flowering and reduce flower and boll dropping in cotton in Karnataka, foliar nutrient sprays and growth regulators are recommended during the flowering stage .The recommended Fertilizers and the method of applying fertilizers for the cotton crop are:

1.Organic Manure:

Irrigated Cotton :
- Apply 4 tonnes of farmyard manure or compost per acre. Alternatively, 0.8 tonnes of poultry manure per acre can be used. Another option is to apply a combination of 1.2 tonnes of Farm Yard Manure, 0.8 tonnes of crop residues, and 0.4 tonnes of vermicompost per acre. These organic manures should be applied two weeks before sowing and at the time of sowing.

Rainfed Cotton :
- Mix 4 tonnes of Farm Yard Manure per acre into the soil 2–3 weeks before sowing cotton. Growing sunhemp between two cotton rows and incorporating it into the soil after 30 days as green manure or mulch improves soil fertility and helps control weeds. This practice can reduce the requirement of recommended chemical fertilizers by up to 50%.

2.Bio-Fertilizers:

- By treating the seeds required per acre with 200 g each of Azospirillum and phosphorus-solubilising bacteria biofertilizers, a saving of 8 kg nitrogen and 4 kg phosphorus from the recommended chemical fertilizers can be achieved.

3.Chemical Fertilizers : Recommended Nutrient Dose per Acre

-For rainfed cotton varieties in dryland regions (Zone 2 and 3), the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 12 kg nitrogen (26 kg urea), 6 kg phosphorus (38 kg SSP), and 6 kg potash (10 kg MOP). 

- In the transitional region (Zone 8), the recommended dose is 16 kg nitrogen (35 kg urea), 10 kg phosphorus (63 kg SSP), and 10 kg potash (17 kg MOP) per acre.

- For rainfed hybrid cotton in the Malnad region (Zone 9), the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 40 kg nitrogen (87 kg urea), 40 kg phosphorus (250 kg SSP), and 40 kg potash (67 kg MOP). 

- In the transitional region (Zone 8), the recommended dose is 32 kg nitrogen (70 kg urea), 16 kg phosphorus (100 kg SSP), and 16 kg potash (27 kg MOP) per acre.

- For Bt cotton, the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 40-50 kg nitrogen (87-109 kg urea), 20-25 kg phosphorus (125 -156 kg SSP), and 20-25 kg potash (33-42 kg MOP). 

- For irrigated hybrid interspecific cotton, the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 60 kg nitrogen (130 kg urea), 30 kg phosphorus (188 kg SSP), and 30 kg potash (50 kg MOP).

- For irrigated hybrid intraspecific cotton, the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 48 kg nitrogen (104 kg urea), 24 kg phosphorus (150 kg SSP), and 24 kg potash (40 kg MOP).

- For irrigated Hybrid Bt cotton intraspecific cotton in the Malaprabha command area, the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 60 kg nitrogen (130 kg urea), 30 kg phosphorus (188 kg SSP), and 30 kg potash (50 kg MOP).

- For Bt cotton intraspecific cotton in the Tungabhadra command area, the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 72 kg nitrogen (157 kg urea), 36 kg phosphorus (225 kg SSP), and 36 kg potash (60 kg MOP).

- For irrigated cotton varieties, the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 32 kg nitrogen (70 kg urea), 16 kg phosphorus (100 kg SSP), and 16 kg potash (27 kg MOP).

- For summer cotton varieties, the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 32 kg nitrogen (70 kg urea), 16 kg phosphorus (100 kg SSP), and 16 kg potash (27 kg MOP).

- For summer hybrid intraspecific cotton, the recommended nutrient dose per acre is 48 kg nitrogen (104 kg urea), 24 kg phosphorus (150 kg SSP), and 24 kg potash (40 kg MOP).
